answer:
Learning to Infer Program Sketches combines neural and symbolic methods by splitting the synthesis task into two stages:

1. **Neural sketch generation**: a recurrent neural network takes the program specification as input and outputs a distribution over candidate **program sketches**—partial programs that may contain holes. The paper describes this as a learned sketch generator \(q_\phi(\text{sketch}\mid X)\). [4]

2. **Symbolic program synthesis**: each candidate sketch is then passed to an **enumerative symbolic synthesizer**, which explicitly searches to fill in the holes and complete the program so it satisfies the specification. [4]

The key idea is that the neural model learns how much detail to put into the sketch: for easier tasks it can propose a more complete sketch, and for harder tasks it can leave more holes for symbolic search to resolve. The paper says this lets the system “learn how much to rely on each component of the system.” [1][4]

So, in short, the neural model proposes sketches and the symbolic component performs explicit search to complete them. [1][4]

Sources used:
- Learning to Infer Program Sketches, DBLP_conf_icml_NyeHTS19.pdf, p. 2
- Learning to Infer Program Sketches, DBLP_journals_corr_abs-1902-06349.pdf, p. 3

Our system consists of two main components: 1) a sketch generator, and 2) a program synthesizer. The sketch generator is a distribution over program sketches given the spec: qφ(sketch|X ). The generator is parametrized by a recurrent neural network, and is trained to assign high probability to sketches which are likely to quickly yield programs satisfying the spec when given to the synthesizer.
